title: What a website redesign actually involves
dek: A realistic week-by-week picture of a small-business redesign, including the parts that always slip and the work only you can do.
body:
Most redesign projects do not fail on design. They fail in the two weeks nobody scheduled, when the build is finished and the words are not.

This is what the work actually looks like from the client side, in the order it happens, so you can tell whether a quote is describing the whole job or only the fun part of it.

Before anyone designs anything

A redesign that starts in a design tool is starting in the middle. The first question is what the site is for, and the honest answer is rarely "to look modern". It is usually to make one specific thing happen: an enquiry, a booking, a phone call.

Write that down before you look at a single layout. Every argument later in the project resolves against it. If you cannot say what the site is supposed to cause, you will spend six weeks discussing shades of blue instead.

The second question is what you already have that is working. Pages that rank, a phone number people call, a form that converts. Those are assets, and a redesign that quietly discards them is not an improvement.

The content problem, which is your problem

Here is the part that gets glossed over in almost every proposal: the words are your job, and they take longer than the build.

An agency can write for you, and a good one will. But the raw material — what you actually do, what makes you different, which questions customers ask before they buy — only exists inside your business. Someone on your side has to sit down and produce it, or approve it, and that person has a day job.

The practical consequence is that you should start content in week one, not week five. A build waiting on copy is the single most common reason a six-week project takes fourteen.

If you do one thing differently on your next redesign, make it this: write the words for your five most important pages before design begins. The design will be better for it, because it will be designed around real content rather than placeholder text.

Design, then build

Design should be reviewed on a screen, at the size people will actually use. A layout approved as a static image on a laptop routinely falls apart on a phone, and most of your visitors are on a phone.

Ask to see the mobile version first. If the answer is that mobile will be handled later, that is a warning: it means the design is being drawn for a desktop and squeezed afterwards, which is not the same thing as designing for a small screen.

During the build, the useful cadence is a weekly look at something real in a browser. Not a screenshot, not a slide — a link you can open on your own phone. Problems found in week two are cheap. The same problems found the day before launch are not.

Two technical things are worth insisting on, and both are much harder to add later than to include from the start. The first is that the search-engine basics are in the build itself: sensible page titles, one heading per page that says what the page is, and clean URLs. The second is that the site works when JavaScript fails, because sometimes it does.

What slips, and why

In roughly the order they cause delays:

  • Content. Covered above. It is nearly always the long pole.
  • Approvals. One person deciding is fast. A committee is not. Name a decision-maker at the start and give them the authority to say yes.
  • Photography. If the design needs real photographs of your premises, your team or your products, that is a shoot, and a shoot needs a date. Stock photography of an office nobody works in is worse than no photograph at all.
  • Access. Domain registrar, hosting, analytics, whatever runs your email. Chasing a password that left with a former employee can cost a week on its own. Find these in week one.
  • The last ten per cent. Legal pages, the thank-you message, the redirects from old URLs. Unglamorous, always underestimated, and the redirects genuinely matter — get them wrong and you lose the rankings you already had.

What not to buy

Some things get sold with redesigns that mostly are not worth your money, including things we could sell you.

A brand-new logo, bundled in, when the existing one is fine. Rebranding is a real project with real reasons; it is not a free extra, and doing it inside a website deadline usually produces a worse logo and a later site.

A custom content management system built specifically for you, when what you publish is a handful of pages a year. You are buying a maintenance obligation that outlives the relationship.

An animation budget spent on the homepage. Motion is worth paying for when it explains something. Motion that exists to prove the agency can do motion costs you load time and, on a mid-range phone, costs your visitor real seconds.

And a launch-day traffic package. Nothing meaningful about search visibility can be bought in a day. What actually helps in week one is having the redirects right, the site indexed, and your Google Business Profile pointing at the new pages.

What to do next

Before you commission anything, do three things. Write down the one action the site is meant to cause. Find out who holds your domain, hosting and analytics. And block out real time, in someone's actual calendar, for the content.

If you want a second opinion on a quote you have been given, or on whether your current site needs a rebuild at all, tell us what is not working and we will tell you honestly. Often the answer is that the site is fine and the problem is that nobody is finding it.

faq.q: How long should a small-business website redesign take?
faq.a: For a straightforward site with a handful of pages, the build itself is usually a matter of weeks. The realistic total depends almost entirely on how quickly content and approvals come back from your side, which is why the same brief can take six weeks for one business and four months for another.

faq.q: Will a redesign hurt my Google rankings?
faq.a: It can, if the old URLs are not redirected to their new equivalents. Every page that had a different address before needs a permanent redirect to the page that replaces it. Ask specifically whether redirect mapping is included, because it is the step most often skipped.

faq.q: Do I need to write the content myself?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but you do need to supply the substance. Someone can interview you and write from that, which is usually the fastest route. What does not work is assuming the words will appear from somewhere while the build proceeds.

If the underlying site is sound and the problem is how it looks and reads, a redesign is cheaper and faster. If it is slow, hard to edit, or built on something nobody maintains any more, you are paying twice by keeping it.
